section_1.title: The Hook: The Musical Analogy
section_1.content: Introduce the concept that any complex periodic signal is just a chord made of pure sine and cosine notes. Use a visual of a 'Spectrum Analyzer' where a messy wave transforms into individual, neat, vertical bars (frequencies).
section_1.example: Imagine a musician playing a complex chord on a piano; the Fourier Series is the sheet music that tells us exactly which individual keys (sines/cosines) were pressed to create that specific sound.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Refresher: Orthogonality
section_2.content: Briefly explain that sine and cosine functions are 'orthogonal'—like the x, y, and z axes in space. This property allows us to isolate specific components of a wave without them interfering with each other.
section_2.example: Visualizing two perpendicular vectors in 3D space: projecting a vector onto the X-axis ignores the Y and Z components, just as integration isolates a single frequency from a complex signal.

section_3.title: The Mathematical Formula: Building Blocks
section_3.content: Present the Fourier Series equation: f(t) = a0/2 + Σ[an cos(nωt) + bn sin(nωt)]. Break down the components visually: the constant 'a0' as the average height, and 'an/bn' as the 'volume' (amplitude) of each harmonic.
section_3.example: An animation showing a square wave being built by adding together sine waves of increasing frequency. First, one bump, then three, then ten—until it looks like a perfect square.

section_4.title: Calculating Coefficients: The Detective Work
section_4.content: Explain how we extract the 'an' and 'bn' coefficients using the integral of the function multiplied by the basis function (sin/cos). This is the 'filtering' process.
section_4.example: A visual 'Sieve' metaphor: passing the complex signal through a filter that only lets through a specific frequency, leaving behind a pure sine wave whose amplitude equals the coefficient.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Real-World Application
section_5.content: Summarize that the Fourier Series turns time-domain signals into frequency-domain data. Connect this to modern technology.
section_5.example: Show how a smartphone compresses a voice recording by identifying the dominant frequencies and discarding the tiny, irrelevant ones, much like a chef removing seeds to make a smooth purée.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Complex signals are chords of pure sine notes.", "A spectrum analyzer reveals these individual frequencies.", "Fourier series is the sheet music of waves."]
        self.setup_layout("The Hook: The Musical Analogy", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display musical score on screen, highlight individual notes in #FFD700.
        note_group = VGroup(
            Circle(radius=0.2, color=WHITE),
            Circle(radius=0.2, color=WHITE),
            Circle(radius=0.2, color=WHITE)
        ).arrange(RIGHT)
        self.place_at_grid(note_group, 'B2', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(Create(note_group))
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFD700"))
        self.play(note_group.animate.set_color("#FFD700"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Introduce harmony staff, show overlapping waves in #00FFFF.
        wave_group = VGroup(
            Axes(x_range=[0, 4, 1], y_range=[-1, 1, 1], axis_config={"include_tip": False}).scale(0.3),
            FunctionGraph(lambda x: 0.5 * np.sin(x * 5), color="#00FFFF"),
            FunctionGraph(lambda x: 0.5 * np.sin(x * 10), color="#00FFFF")
        )
        self.place_at_grid(wave_group, 'D2', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(FadeIn(wave_group))
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#00FFFF"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Fade out notes, bring in vector representation in #FFFFFF.
        self.play(FadeOut(note_group))
        vector = Arrow(ORIGIN, UP*1, color="#FFFFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(vector, 'B2', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(GrowArrow(vector))
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        self.wait(2)
